text: Proofing bread dough: leave the shaped dough in a warm, draught-free spot until it has nearly doubled in size. Press it gently with a floured finger; if the dent springs back slowly, the loaf is ready to bake.

A sourdough starter is flour and water colonised by wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria. Feed it equal weights of flour and water once a day at room temperature, or once a week if it lives in the fridge.
Cook dried pasta in plenty of well-salted boiling water, about ten grams of salt per litre. Keep a cup of the starchy cooking water: a splash of it helps a sauce cling to the noodles.

For fluffy long-grain rice, rinse the grains until the water runs clear, then simmer one part rice with one and a half parts water under a tight lid for twelve minutes and let it stand off the heat for ten.

A whetstone sharpens a chef's knife: soak the stone, hold the blade at fifteen to twenty degrees and draw it across the coarse side, then the fine side. A honing steel only straightens the edge between sharpenings.

Season a cast iron pan by wiping a very thin layer of oil over it and baking it upside down at high heat for an hour. After cooking, wash it with hot water, dry it on the stove and rub in a drop of oil so it does not rust.

The browning of seared meat, toast and roasted coffee is the Maillard reaction between amino acids and sugars, which speeds up above about 140 C. Pat food dry and do not crowd the pan, so it sears instead of steaming.

Mayonnaise and vinaigrette are emulsions: tiny droplets of oil held in a water-based liquid. Egg yolk and mustard act as emulsifiers; pour the oil in slowly while whisking so the sauce does not split.
If a mayonnaise splits, put a fresh egg yolk or a spoon of warm water in a clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce into it a few drops at a time until it thickens again.
Blanching means boiling vegetables briefly and then plunging them into iced water. It keeps green beans and broccoli bright green, firms their texture and is the usual step before freezing them.

A brown stock starts with roasted bones and vegetables covered with cold water and simmered gently for several hours. Skim the foam that rises, and never let it boil hard: boiling makes the stock cloudy.
For eggs with set whites and soft, jammy yolks, lower them into boiling water for six and a half minutes, then cool them in iced water. Older eggs peel more easily than very fresh ones.
Bacteria multiply fastest between 5 C and 60 C, the danger zone. Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate them within two hours, and cook poultry until the thickest part reaches 74 C.
Baking soda is pure sodium bicarbonate and needs an acid such as buttermilk or yogurt to make a batter rise. Baking powder already contains its own acid, so it works with plain milk.
Flours without gluten, such as rice, buckwheat or almond flour, cannot trap gas on their own. Gluten-free breads add a binder such as psyllium husk or xanthan gum to hold the crumb together.
Keep soft herbs like parsley, coriander and basil fresh by trimming the stems and standing them in a glass of water. Wrap hardy herbs such as rosemary and thyme in a damp paper towel in the fridge.
To make caramel, heat sugar until it melts and turns amber, around 170 C. A wet caramel starts with a little water and is easier to control; swirl the pan rather than stirring, so no crystals form.
Rest a roast or a steak for five to ten minutes after cooking. The juices settle back into the fibres, so less of them runs out onto the board when you slice it.
Sous vide cooking seals food in a bag and holds it in a water bath at an exact temperature, so a steak cooks evenly from edge to centre. Finish it in a very hot pan for a browned crust.
Kosher salt has large flakes and less salt per spoonful than fine table salt, so swap one for the other by weight, not by volume. Flaky sea salt is best sprinkled on at the end for crunch.
